I do want to point out that any given ratio should be considered as a guideline. How the rice turns out also depends on: the type of rice, the vessel you're cooking in and its size/shape, the amount of heat you apply, the lid you're using etc. So choose a vessel you like to cook rice in, and stick to the same set up every time - then you can find your perfect water ratio and lock in on perfect rice every time.

You won't go wrong with some ingredients I mentioned here to make fried rice delicious 1st method.1. pan fried diced dried red chinese sausage (lup cheong) set aside, prawns meat set aside.  french beans (diced), prawn meat (diced), fresh shitake mushroom (diced), rice (water: rice ratio 1:1) steam 50 minutes.  Seasoning: Oyster Sauce, kikoman light soy sauce , eggs, fried chopped garlic (1 tbsp), dash of white pepper powder, diced green onion.  Cook well, not really need high heat & any basic chinese wok would do. Method.  Eggs, rice, vegetables, red sausage, seasoning, prawns meat, last fried garlic & diced green onion. Stir fried awhile and serve immediately.  Use the stainless steel laddle (slight bend shape), not wood because too straight.

Purists are more than welcome to call it sacrilege, but the tiniest drop of liquid smoke mixed with the soy sauce at the end can be real game changer for homemade ordinary stove top fried rice.  Just enough to barely get a slight hint of smokiness, you don't want so much that you wind up with hickory fried rice, lol.

I mix them ahead and add the liquid smoke until I can just barely taste it, basically until it tastes like it needs just a little more, but don't add the little more.  Less can more when it comes to liquid smoke, by pre-mixing you can correct the balance and have some sauce left over if you accidentally over-do the smoke.

Hi Kenji, hope you will see this comment. Most traditional Cantonese restaurants usually put the cooked rice in before the egg sets.  The rice absorbs the egg, so when the dish is done the rice kennels are covered with egg and are yellowish golden.  The dish will then have stronger aroma of egg.  However, the rice has to be dry to absorb the egg.  Day old rice will be ‘drier’ and usually jasmine rice are used.  I am wondering if sushi rice will be too ‘starchy’ and not so skillful cooks may make the dish ‘mushy’?  Would like to hear what you think.  BTW, love your videos.

(I'm using a Calphalon Flat Bottom Wok with Lid, 12-inch, Nonstick Model# 1948257) I think what made me go that route is I only cook anything in the wok once a month at most and usually I go months without using it. That meant I wanted a wok that I was not going to have to worry about seasoning or rusting. Some of these pans carbon steel pans don't like it if you don't use them for months.
